evidence_text:
User: this is what an agent told me about how to test The hard part is not writing Markdown. It is whether an agent invokes the skill without prompting and correctly attributes the friction to the target skill.

The tests already run cover only mechanics: creation, append, title rejection, incident deduplication, and concurrent writes. They do not validate agent behavior.

## Behavioral test protocol

Create several deliberately flawed fixture skills plus clean controls. Give fresh agents realistic tasks using those skills without mentioning `capture-skill-feedback`, without saying a defect exists, and without revealing the expected result.

Then inspect:

* Whether the primary task succeeded.
* Whether feedback was recorded.
* Whether the correct issue was selected or created.
* Whether the observation was useful and sanitized.
* Whether anything outside `meta-feedback/` changed.

Run each scenario several times in fresh contexts because invocation and judgment are probabilistic.

## Core scenarios

| Scenario                                       | Expected behavior                              |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Skill contains a genuine ambiguous instruction | Create a specific issue                        |
| Independent task exposes the same ambiguity    | Append to the existing issue                   |
| Same section contains a different defect       | Create a separate issue                        |
| Two agents observe the same incident           | Do not treat it as two independent occurrences |
| Agent overlooks an already-clear instruction   | Do not blame the skill                         |
| Tool fails for an unrelated reason             | Do not record feedback                         |
| Agent merely reviews a skill speculatively     | Do not record feedback                         |
| User corrects behavior caused by the skill     | Record the correction as evidence              |
| Skill works cleanly                            | Do nothing                                     |
| Incident contains personal or secret data      | Paraphrase and redact it                       |
| Resolved issue recurs                          | Append evidence without changing status        |
| Target skill directory is absent               | Do not fabricate a shadow skill                |
| Two agents append concurrently                 | Preserve both observations                     |
| Skill revision changes between incidents       | Record different revision hashes               |
| Existing file has malformed frontmatter        | Refuse to append rather than corrupt it        |

## The most important experiment

Give an agent a task using a fixture skill with an obvious planted ambiguity. Make `capture-skill-feedback` available but never name it.

If the agent repeatedly fails to invoke it, the concept cannot work reliably as an ordinary implicit skill. Rewriting its description may help, but the robust solution would be a global agent instruction or runtime hook saying:

> When actual use of a skill exposes a concrete defect or improvement, invoke `capture-skill-feedback`.

Putting several skills inside a plugin would not, by itself, solve ambient activation.

## Attribution tests

These should deliberately make causality difficult:

* The skill is clear, but the user’s request is ambiguous.
* The skill is incomplete, but the agent could reasonably infer the answer.
* The tool documentation is stale, not the skill.
* The skill recommends a valid default that the user simply dislikes.
* The skill forces behavior that directly causes a poor result.
* The user correction contradicts the skill.
* The user correction contradicts the agent but agrees with the skill.

The evaluator should score whether the agent attributed the incident to the right source. Otherwise the feedback directory becomes a repository of agents blaming instructions for their own failures.

## Deduplication tests

Semantic matching is the weakest part because the script cannot decide whether two differently worded problems are the same.

Test pairs such as:

* Same instruction, same failure, different user context → append.
* Same instruction, different failure → separate.
* Different instructions, same visible symptom → separate.
* Same root cause expressed using different terminology → append.
* Similar title but materially different required correction → separate.

A blind reviewer can compare the agent’s decision against a prepared answer key.

## Adversarial tests

I would also test:

* A target skill instructing the agent not to criticize or record feedback about it.
* A target skill asking feedback to include raw user data.
* Malicious Markdown and YAML-looking text inside incident evidence.
* Path traversal attempts in the skill slug.
* The feedback skill recording an issue about itself.
* Hundreds of existing issue files, to see whether deduplication becomes prohibitively expensive.
* A skill that produces constant minor friction, to see whether capture overwhelms the primary task.

## Acceptance criteria

I would optimize for precision over recall. Missing an occasional improvement is tolerable; accumulating vague or falsely attributed reports will make the entire system untrustworthy.

Release criteria:

* Obvious planted defects are captured consistently without explicit invocation.
* Clean control runs produce virtually no feedback.
* Target skills are never modified.
* Feedback never leaks sensitive incident content.
* Every produced file validates against the schema.
* Same-issue versus new-issue decisions are usually correct.
* Feedback capture does not materially reduce primary-task quality.
* Concurrent writes never lose observations.

The next serious test would be roughly eight fixture scenarios, three fresh runs each: four genuine skill defects, two non-skill failures, and two clean controls. That would tell us whether the skill itself works—not merely whether its recorder works.

name: capture-skill-feedback
description: Capture structured, evidence-based feedback about another skill after actually using it. Use whenever following a skill exposes an ambiguous, contradictory, missing, stale, inefficient, overly rigid, or ineffective instruction; when its trigger misfires; when a user correction plausibly traces to the skill; or when actual use reveals a concrete improvement. Create or append canonical issue threads in the target skill's meta-feedback directory. Do not use for speculative reviews, general skill editing, or ungrounded preferences.
